title: AVERAGE: mean of a score list

screens.prompt: In B7, work out the class average of the five scores.

hints.syntax: =AVERAGE(B2:B6): one function, one range, no plus signs.
hints.func-average: Use AVERAGE. Adding the scores and dividing by five by hand works here and breaks the moment a student leaves.
hints.require-ref: Point the formula at the score column instead of typing the number you worked out.
hints.value: That does not match the scores. AVERAGE divides by the count of numbers, so check nothing extra got included.
hints.error: #DIV/0! means AVERAGE found no numbers at all: the range is pointing at blank cells or at the header word rather than at the five scores. Text is skipped silently, not averaged.

reject.why: the arithmetic is right but SUM is not AVERAGE
types the scores into AVERAGE instead of pointing at B2:B6

docs.explain: AVERAGE adds the numbers and divides by how many it found. The five scores here are 85, 90, 88, 92 and 87.5, which come to 442.5, and 442.5 ÷ 5 = 88.5. The useful difference from typing the arithmetic yourself is the denominator. AVERAGE counts only cells holding a number, so a sixth student with no score leaves the divisor at 5. A blank cell is skipped, a zero is not. That is why a class average can be wrong while every individual score looks right.

errors.text: The range you pointed at holds no numbers at all, for example a column of names.
A cell inside the range contains text that AVERAGE cannot read as a number.
Averages built as SUM(...)/6 where the range holds five students drift the moment someone joins or leaves.

docs.atWork: Score averages, average order value, average handle time: the same function covers all of them. The professional habit is to let AVERAGE count, so the number survives a blank row.
docs.outcome: Turn five scores into one class average that updates itself.

seo.title: AVERAGE in Excel: the mean of a column
seo.description: AVERAGE divides the total by the count of numbers, so a blank cell never drags the mean down. Five scores average 88.5, and the page shows why.
